sources.news_title: Donald Trump stands by Pete Hegseth in shock briefing as he faces impeachment vote
sources.text:
Donald Trump has pledged to stand by Pete Hegeth as he faces an impeachment vote.
Republican Congressman and foe of the President, Thomas Massie, introduced articles of impeachment on the House floor on Monday, alleging that the Secretary of War has violated US Constitution.
He told the House: "By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable."
The Commander-in-Chief, in an impromptu press conference featuring UFC chief Dana White, said he would stand by Mr Hegseth even if he was impeached, and had harsh words for the Kentucky Representative who has been a thorn in his side in his second term.
"He's a loser," he said. "He shouldn't be taking up the time of Congress or the Senate."
"We could come up with the best bill we could come up with, and he would always vote against," the President added. "There's something wrong with him."
The motion introduced by Mr Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, is likely to fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January.
But he may be hoping that disgruntled members of his party, who have also not been re-elected after the so-called "blue tsunami", will support the impeachment.
Washington Bureau Chief at the Guardian, David Smith, told GB News it could be a "close-run" thing.
He said: "We've obviously got Thomas Massie on the Republican side, and some indications that a handful of other Republicans might join him.
"Don Bacon and others have indicated they're not so staunch supporters of Pete Hegseth anymore."
Mr Hegesth, for his part, said he was "not worried about that" and plans to hold a news conference on the impeachment motion on Tuesday.
LATEST US POLITICS
Earlier in the week, he released a defiant video declaring that a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" had introduced "sham articles of impeachment" against him.
"Just like they tried against President Trump twice," he said. "You see, their policies don’t work, so their obsession with political theatre disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents.
"It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me."
Mr Massie warned that his articles of impeachment were "a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year", adding that new Congressmen would hold "hearings and trials".
New York congressman Hakeem Jeffries has already said he is a "hard yes" to the vote.
Mr Smith told GB News the Kentucky Representative may have launched the impeachment vote now as a way to remain in the political conversation.
He added: "My understanding is that if a vote is passed, it does not die with this current Congress. It will carry on into the next one.
"So there may not be a total escape for Hegseth. And I would say, probably whatever happens here, as long as he is still in office, which will presumably be the case, then Democrats will still pursue their investigations, their oversight hearings, particularly into the origins of the Iran war, to ordering air strikes on boats in the Caribbean and so on. And they will enjoy holding him up to fierce scrutiny."
Also at the previously unannounced press briefing, UFC boss Mr White, who was floated as Press Secretary, took questions from the media but ultimately confirmed he would not be the White House's new spokesman.
He told reporters he had "zero political aspirations", but when answering a reporter's question, said the current President would likely defeat former President Joe Biden in a mixed martial arts fight.

sources.news_title: Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
sources.text:
Rep. Thomas Massie has reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting up a vote in the House of Representatives in the next two days.
The Kentucky Republican’s resolution accuses Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors and lists eight specific charges against him.
The allegations include:
- 3 charges for illegally waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution
- 1 charge for ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties
- 1 charge for overseeing “extrajudicial killings” in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean with strikes on alleged drug boats
- 1 charge for suppressing free speech, brought in connection to the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for a video telling service members they can refuse illegal orders
- 1 charge for the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization
- 1 charge for illegally waging war against Yemen in violation of the War Powers Resolution
Hegseth defended his record at the Pentagon in a video released last Thursday, dismissing Massie’s effort as “sham articles of impeachment.”
“Didn’t work against President Trump and it won’t work with me,” Hegseth said.
Speaking to reporters during an impromptu press briefing on Monday, Trump expressed support for his embattled Defense Secretary.
“I’ll stand by him,” Trump said. “He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won.”
Massie has long been a staunch critic of Hegseth. During the GOP primary, Hegseth campaigned on behalf of Ed Gallrein, who went on to defeat Massie.
In response to Hegseth calling him a “disgruntled defeated congressman,” Massie told reporters on Monday: “Well, he’s right about one thing — I’m a defeated congressman. I’m not disgruntled.”
He added: “I’m being polite here. What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing someone, really. You don’t go to prison, you don’t go to jail, you don’t pay a fine. When the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious.”
Massie said the effort also underscores the need to litigate whether Congress has real war powers or not. The war powers resolution has largely been ignored by presidents of both parties.
“What’s at heart here is the balance of power between the executive branch and Congress,” he said.
Massie first sought to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterm elections, prompting Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to call an early recess to avoid the vote. That caused the resolution to expire, which is why Massie reintroduced the resolution Monday.
Presumptive next House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has already signaled support for an impeachment push against Hegseth.
Even Republican members who oppose impeaching Hegseth have said the Trump administration could do a better job making the case to Congress and the public about what the plan is for the Iran war going forward.
Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio., indicated to NPR that impeachment would be hypocritical given that administrations going back to the Korean War have largely ignored Congress’ war powers efforts.
“I think trying to scapegoat Pete Hegseth is just the status quo politics in Washington,” he said. “I think it would be a mistake to impeach.”
Davidson said lawmakers who want changes are better off trying to leverage the power of the purse to withhold money from the conflict.
There could be sufficient votes to impeach Hegseth in the House, with the support of all Democrats, Massie, and a handful of Republicans. However, it is unlikely to clear the higher Senate threshold for convicting and removing Hegseth from office — which requires two-thirds of the Senate.
NPR’s Eric McDaniel contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Republican moves to impeach US defence chief Hegseth for waging Iran war without Congress
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 — A Republican lawmaker moved yesterday to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, setting up a potentially explosive vote in Congress days after President Donald Trump’s party suffered a crushing midterm defeat.
Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorisation and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
The Republican-controlled House could vote as early as tomorrow, with some lawmakers from Trump’s party signaling they might join Democrats in backing the charges.
Trump threw his support behind Hegseth yesterday, declaring he had done a “good job” and “won” wars in Venezuela and Iran — referring to the lightning raid that captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January, and the unresolved eight-month conflict with Tehran.
Asked what would happen if Hegseth is impeached, Trump told reporters: “Yeah, I’ll stand by him.”
Impeachment would be a humiliating blow for the Trump administration, but would not automatically remove Hegseth. Conviction requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate — a much higher hurdle, even after Democrats take control in January.
The move has gathered momentum since Tuesday’s midterms, when Democrats swept both chambers amid voter anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices.
Republicans retain control until the new Congress takes office on January 3, but their defeat has fuelled recriminations. Defeated Republicans could skip votes, making impeachment easier to pass.
‘Hard yes’
Massie, a Trump critic who lost his primary to a candidate backed by the president, is using a special procedure requiring the House to consider his resolution within two legislative days.
Hegseth had “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders” by waging war without congressional approval, Massie said on the House floor.
His articles allege violations of the 1973 War Powers Resolution, as well as misconduct involving civilian casualties and operations in Yemen and Venezuela.
The Pentagon has rejected the allegations.
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to become speaker in January, said Sunday he was a “hard yes” on impeachment.
“The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran,” Jeffries told ABC News.
“Pete Hegseth has got to go.”
Unlikely removal
Some Republicans are wavering. Arkansas congressman French Hill said he wanted to hear the debate before deciding whether the accusations merited impeachment.
Under the Constitution, the House can bring impeachment charges by a simple majority. The Senate then holds a trial, with two-thirds of senators present needed to convict and remove the official.
Democrats would need substantial Republican support even after they take the Senate majority. Only two Cabinet secretaries have been impeached in US history, and neither was removed by the Senate.
Hegseth has called Massie’s effort a “sham” and dismissed him as a “disgruntled” congressman. The Pentagon has scheduled a rare Hegseth press briefing Tuesday, while Trump yesterday dismissed Massie as a “stone cold loser.”
Republican congressman Don Bacon questioned Massie’s reasoning but argued Hegseth deserved impeachment for withholding aid to Ukraine and forcing out or blocking promotions for around 80 senior military officers.
“There’s a bunch of us have been talking about it,” Bacon told CNN, urging Hegseth to resign. — AFP

sources.news_title: Massie Files Hegseth Impeachment; Vote Due by Wednesday
sources.text:
Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky refiled his resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the House floor on Monday, the first day the chamber was in session after the midterm elections, forcing a House vote within two legislative days, which means by Wednesday. The move came a day after House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he is a "hard yes" and as House Republican leaders braced for enough defections in their own ranks to pass it. House Speaker Mike Johnson said impeaching a Cabinet secretary during hostilities abroad would be a "terrible, terrible look." President Donald Trump, who said Thursday he has "every intention" of keeping Hegseth, said Monday he would stand by him even if he is impeached. Vice President JD Vance has said the party lost the midterm elections because of the war in Iran, and no vote count has been published.
Massie, who lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger and leaves office in January, had said he would file the resolution unless Hegseth resigned first. He first introduced the articles in September, reading a 34-page resolution with eight articles of impeachment on the House floor for more than an hour. The articles accuse Hegseth of waging hostilities against Iran without congressional authorization, in violation of the War Powers Resolution, of ignoring laws meant to minimize civilian casualties, and of overseeing what Massie calls extrajudicial killings in strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats; they also refer to military actions in Yemen and Venezuela. The vote never took place, because Johnson canceled the remaining floor votes before the chamber left for the midterm recess, and the resolution expired, which is why Massie refiled it Monday and read the eight articles on the floor again. Because the resolution is privileged, House rules require a vote within two legislative days of its filing. Leaders can instead move to table the resolution or refer it to a committee, either of which takes a simple majority and would effectively kill it, a tactic Massie warned Johnson might try. Most privileged resolutions die on a procedural vote, but several Republicans said this one could pass with the party's losses fresh. An impeachment needs only a simple majority in the House, while conviction requires two-thirds of the Senate.
Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker in January, said in a Sunday television interview that he is "a hard yes" on the resolution and that House Democrats will "have that conversation" at a Tuesday morning conference, their first gathering in Washington since the election. Democrats are widely expected to support the articles. House Republican leaders are bracing for enough GOP defections to impeach Hegseth when the measure comes to a vote this week, according to reports, because Republicans who lost their seats on Tuesday have little left to lose and support for Hegseth has eroded since the war began. Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska said he was undecided.
The effort draws on private anger among Republicans. Several lawmakers have said Hegseth oversold the United States' ability to win the war quickly and easily and encouraged Trump to launch it without a clear exit strategy, according to Republican sources. A former senior Pentagon official said "the pivot is starting" on both the war and the defense secretary. Republican strategists say the party's problems extend beyond Hegseth, and that Trump, as commander in chief, made the final decision to attack Iran in February.
Trump's public position has not wavered. "I have every intention to keep him," he said Thursday morning, adding that he receives calls from people unhappy with Hegseth but does not "understand why." Asked about the impeachment effort, he called Massie "very destructive." On Wednesday, he had said Hegseth was doing "a very good job," and on Sunday night he again endorsed him, saying Hegseth is "guilty of two things, basically winning two wars," and urged Democrats to "get back to the country." On Monday, Trump told CNN he would stand by Hegseth even if the House impeaches him and called Massie a loser. Trump has reportedly asked advisers and allies whether Hegseth should stay and who might succeed him, a report the White House has not confirmed. The administration has a short window to act: Democrats will hold a Senate majority beginning Jan. 3, which would make confirming a new defense secretary harder.
Hegseth's spokesman, Sean Parnell, said the secretary "will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists." Hegseth dismissed the impeachment push as "noise" on Monday and told reporters that he and his team are not worried; Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended him as doing a "great job" and called the effort "unfair." Earlier, Hegseth said in remarks that attacks on him are "not going to work," according to a video clip circulating online. Democrats have said they plan to investigate the Pentagon's conduct of the Iran war, the dismissal of senior officers and the military's strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker in January, wrote on social media Thursday, "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?" Trump has since accused Democrats of "extortion" over their promised investigations and impeachment talk and directed Attorney General Todd Blanche to look into it, a claim Democrats reject.
The dispute sits inside a wider fight over who is responsible for the election result. On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance published a long post on X saying that many people who voted for Trump and Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats this year. He said a pollster he trusts told him the top reasons were ending the war, focusing on the cost of living, putting "America First" and changing the U.S. relationship with Israel. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote, adding, "The president himself said so last night," and that anyone who thinks losing the Senate for six years was worth it should "argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay." Donald Trump Jr. replied that every word of the post was accurate, with three hundred-point emojis.
Trump has said the war was part of the reason Republicans lost. On Tuesday, he said Iran "was a piece of it," and on Thursday he said he would "do it again," defending the decision as necessary to stop Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. An exit poll found that 74% of voters considered the war a crucial or major factor in their vote, according to one analysis. The war began Feb. 28, when the United States and Israel struck Iran and killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, and it has since expanded into a blockade of Iranian ports and a series of limited strikes, including strikes on Qeshm Island last Monday and again overnight Sunday, according to Iranian state media.
Iran's leaders have used the dispute. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X that Americans "said NO TO WAR," and Iran's security chief said Tehran had inflicted a political defeat on Trump. Analysts said Vance's post, which listed changing the relationship with Israel among the causes, signals both a break with Trump's strategy and an effort to position himself for a 2028 presidential run. Vance did not say he disagreed with the president directly, and his post said he remained hopeful.
For Hegseth, the question is whether a Republican House that has defended him for months will now repudiate him, and whether Trump decides he is more useful as a defender or as a casualty. If the House impeaches him, the case would go to a Senate that is Republican-controlled until January, where conviction would require 67 votes, a threshold that even Democrats' larger majority in the next Congress would not reach without Republican support. If Trump removes Hegseth or Hegseth resigns first, Massie has said he will not reintroduce the articles.
The next signals come quickly. Massie filed the resolution on Monday, House Democrats meet Tuesday morning to settle their position, and House Republicans choose their leader on Nov. 10. A floor vote must follow by Wednesday unless leaders move to table the resolution or refer it to a committee, either of which would show how many Republicans are willing to break ranks. Whether Trump holds to his word on Hegseth, whether enough Republicans split on the war to carry the vote, and whether Vance and the White House reconcile their positions will shape how the administration approaches Iran in the lame-duck weeks.

Pentagon chief Hegseth expected to face House impeachment vote this week

Pentagon chief Hegseth expected to face House impeachment vote this week
Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass but conviction appears unlikely.
WASHINGTON: Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, calls himself the secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and "woke" when he took office last year. Now, with an expected House impeachment vote this week, he could soon share something in common with an actual secretary of war.
William Belknap, who held that title in 1876, became the first, and to date only, civilian leader of the US military to be impeached by Congress.
US Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment on Monday (Nov 9), setting off a two-day clock for a potential House vote on charges including waging war against Iran without congressional approval and other abuses of power.
Massie, addressing reporters, cautioned that Republican leadership could try to avoid a straight vote on impeachment by trying to dismiss it with a procedural motion.
"They may try to get out of an actual vote on the substance of this. We should have a vote and a rigorous debate on these eight articles of impeachment," he told a press conference.
Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with President Donald Trump’s Republicans still controlling the House until Democrats take over on Jan 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, however, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats.
US President Donald Trump, in an interview with Reuters on Monday, strongly defended Hegseth, pointing to the US military's performance in Iran and Venezuela: "Well, he won two wars. I don't know how you can impeach him."
House Speaker Mike Johnson opposed the effort, saying impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad” would be “a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see”.
Voter anger over the war helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week's midterm elections, intensifying Republican divisions over a conflict that Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned and Hegseth has defended as “courageous and historic”.
Accused of taking huge kickbacks, Belknap handed President Ulysses Grant his resignation ahead of his scheduled impeachment vote and, according to a Senate history, “burst into tears”. The House impeached him anyway, but the Senate later acquitted him after falling short of the required two-thirds majority.
By contrast, Hegseth is promising to stay and fight.
HEGSETH SAYS HE IS NOT WORRIED
Hegseth has mounted a social media campaign, saying in a defiant video message last week that he would not back down. He also drew a comparison to Trump, who was impeached twice, saying: "It didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."
Asked if he had enough Republican support to defeat the impeachment push, Hegseth said on Monday: "We're not worried about that." He announced a Tuesday press conference, his first at the Pentagon since May.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also White House national security adviser, called the impeachment push "unfair," telling reporters: "I think Pete's done a good job. I really do."
Trump, speaking with Reuters, extolled Hegseth's performance in the Iran war, which is at an impasse, and with Venezuela, where the US military deposed that country's president, Nicolás Maduro, in a surprise January commando raid on his compound in the Venezuelan capital.
"Well, what about impeaching the people from Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq and all of that, where we fought forever and nothing happened?" Trump asked.
DEFENCE SPENDING AT RISK?
Some Republican lawmakers have expressed concern that if Hegseth stays, his strained relationship with Congress will undermine the Trump administration's push for a US$1.5 trillion defence spending package.
Massie, a Trump critic who is leaving office in January, warned in a statement on Monday that impeachment would be "much gentler" than what's in store for Hegseth once Democrats take control in January.
"They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," Massie said.
Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth over issues including the firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and other senior leaders.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Sunday he was a "hard yes" on a measure to impeach Hegseth.
US Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is expected to become majority leader, said on Monday the Senate needs to put Hegseth on trial.
"Hegseth waged this war illegally, in open defiance of the Constitution and multiple War Powers Resolutions this Congress passed to end the fighting," he said.
Massie's articles of impeachment accuse Hegseth of "high crimes and misdemeanours" ranging from waging the Iran war to various alleged abuses of power, including violating the free speech rights of US Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat.
Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Kelly after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence urged US troops to refuse illegal orders. Hegseth accused them of sedition, something Trump at the time said in a social media post was "punishable by DEATH!"

sources.news_title: GOP Rep. Massie introduces impeachment articles against Hegseth
sources.text:
Nov. 9 (UPI) — Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the U.S. war on Iran. A House vote on the articles could happen this week.
Massie originally introduced impeachment articles against Hegseth in September, but Speaker of the House Mike Johnson dismissed lawmakers early, avoiding a vote on the issue before the midterm elections. Now that they have been reintroduced, Republican leaders have two days to schedule a vote.
The updated resolution includes eight charges against Hegseth, some of which accuse him of abusing the powers of the Defense Department and waging war against Iran without congressional approval, an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.
Charges also include ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties, presiding over extrajudicial killings (referring to strikes on alleged drug boats), suppressing free speech (in reference to using department authority to threaten Sen. Mark Kelly over his comments on questioning unlawful military orders) and kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader (referring to the kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela without congressional or legal authority).
“By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said.
“Secretary Hegseth’s constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran,” he said. “He is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders and to intimidate critics of the Trump administration by retaliating against them for exercising free speech. If we are to remain true to our oath to ‘support and defend the Constitution of the United States,’ the House of Representatives must act.”
Hegseth said he wasn’t worried about the charges and that he plans to hold a press conference on the impeachment effort Tuesday morning. In a social media post last week, he called Massie “a disgruntled, defeated congressman” and said the charges are “all about the politics of personal destruction.”
“Didn’t work against President Trump and won’t work against me,” Hegseth said.
Some other Republicans have also questioned Hegseth’s actions in Iran, though they’ve also questioned if he deserves to be impeached.
“We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran,” said Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., who leads the House Oversight Committee. “No one’s happy about Iran. I think the Republican voters are more unhappy about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters.”
Hegseth would be the third U.S. Cabinet secretary to be impeached. Neither of the other two, William Belknap in 1876 and Alejandro Majorkas in 2024, was removed from office. Belknap was acquitted by the Senate and the charges against Majorkas were dropped.

sources.news_title: Massie Introduces Eight Articles of Impeachment Against Hegseth, Setting Up House Showdown Over Iran War
sources.text:
Rep. Thomas Massie has renewed his effort to remove Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of violating congressional war powers, authorizing unlawful military operations and abusing his authority as Republican leaders face a possible impeachment vote this week.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., formally introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the House floor Monday, Nov. 9, accusing the Pentagon chief of violating federal law and the Constitution through military operations in Iran, Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean.
The move revives an impeachment effort that Republican leaders delayed in September and could force the House to act as early as Wednesday, with Democrats preparing to take control of Congress in January.
Massie presented the charges during an extended House floor speech, reading from a 34-page impeachment resolution published by his congressional office.
The resolution accuses Hegseth of unlawfully conducting military operations without congressional authorization, disregarding restrictions imposed by the War Powers Resolution and authorizing actions that Massie argues violated constitutional protections.
“In all of this, Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense and subversive of constitutional government,” Massie declared in the resolution.
The Kentucky Republican first introduced impeachment articles in September, but House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., recessed the chamber before lawmakers could vote. The legislation subsequently expired, requiring Massie to restart the process.
Monday’s filing renews the procedural timetable under which the House must address a privileged impeachment resolution within two legislative days. Republican leaders could bring the measure to a vote, seek to table it or refer it to committee.
According to NPR’s coverage of the proceedings, the eight charges include three allegations involving the U.S. war against Iran.
Massie contends that Hegseth violated the War Powers Resolution of 1973 by directing military operations without a declaration of war, specific congressional authorization or an attack on the United States establishing an immediate national emergency.
The impeachment resolution also accuses Hegseth of continuing hostilities after the expiration of statutory time limits and disregarding congressional resolutions directing the withdrawal of American forces.
Another article alleges that Hegseth failed to comply with legal requirements intended to minimize civilian casualties during military operations.
Additional charges concern U.S. strikes against suspected drug-trafficking vessels in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean, which Massie characterizes as extrajudicial killings.
The resolution also challenges the military operation that captured former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and alleges violations of federal law involving military actions in Yemen.
A separate article accuses Hegseth of suppressing free speech through the Pentagon’s response to Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., after Kelly participated in a video reminding military personnel of their obligation to refuse unlawful orders.
During Monday’s proceedings, Massie argued that Hegseth had improperly exercised military authority belonging to Congress.
“Secretary Hegseth has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office,” Massie said while reading the resolution.
The congressman later told reporters that his effort was intended to establish accountability for executive branch decisions involving the use of military force.
“What’s at heart here is the balance of power between the executive branch and Congress,” Massie said.
The impeachment effort has intensified following Republican losses in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which have placed additional scrutiny on the administration’s conduct of the Iran war.

A vote in the House of Representatives could take place as early as this week.

Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced the impeachment articles on Monday, triggering a two-day window for a possible House vote. "They may try to get out of an actual vote on the substance of this. We should have a vote and a rigorous debate on these eight articles," Massie told reporters.

"Well, he won two wars. I don't know how you can impeach him," Trump said.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting the stage for a dramatic vote on whether to remove one of the Trump administration’s most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.
The impeachment resolution was introduced by Massie, a Kentucky Republican, as soon as the House opened for the first day of sessions after the midterms. It largely focuses on the war in Iran but also includes references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie said the secretary’s actions amount to “high crimes and misdemeanors” and his leadership at the Pentagon “thus warrants impeachment.”
A vote in the House could come by mid-week, putting pressure on Republicans — many of whom blamed their election wipeout on the Iran war — but next steps are highly uncertain.
House Speaker Mike Johnson had tried to prevent this outcome, and warned lawmakers against impeaching the Defense secretary while the U.S. is engaged in military actions in the Middle East.
“Impeaching a Cabinet secretary right now, especially the Department of War in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that,” Johnson, a Republican, said as he opened the chamber.
“We don’t impeach Cabinet secretaries for political gain or for cheap tricks, and I think that’s what this is and I think everybody knows it.”
Most House Democrats are expected to support impeaching Hegseth, with Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries saying over the weekend it’s time for the Defense secretary to go.
If the House votes to impeach Hegseth, it would next go to the Senate for a potential trial. Republicans remain in the majority in both chambers, until the new Congress convenes in January with Democrats in control.
Hegseth issues his own defense and prepares for a fight
Hegseth maintains he’s eager to litigate the military actions that he and President Donald Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela’s previous leaders.
“If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you’re taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic,” Hegseth told reporters Monday, using the military code names for the Iran war and campaign of strikes to halt the Houthis’ attacks on shipping in the Middle East.
Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference on Tuesday — his first in over 180 days — on the impeachment threat. His last briefing was in May, and he has not held one on the Iran war, strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats or other U.S. military actions since then.
The Pentagon chief is bearing the brunt of anger and calls for his ouster after the Iran war and its economic impact contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections that cost the party control of Congress.
Hegseth waves off impeachment push as ‘noise’
Hegseth, after giving a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, brushed aside the impeachment push.
“There’s a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success,” he told reporters. He added that “if we want to litigate” the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, “I’m happy to do it all day long.”
“My team, we’re not worried about the noise — it’s what I told the troops, too — ‘don’t worry about the noise,’” he said.
Asked about Vice President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the massive GOP losses in the election, Hegseth noted that Trump said he would do it again, and “I agree.”
He largely repeated a line that Secretary of State Marco Rubio said to reporters a day earlier: “It doesn’t have to be necessarily popular, but it can be necessary.”
Hegseth argued that the war was necessary because “someone had to confront the Iranian regime’s pursuit of a nuclear weapon” and said “the choice was don’t act and wish it away or take a bold move.”
Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Sunday night.
“He’s guilty of two things, basically winning two wars,” Trump said. “I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it’s awfully hard to say let’s impeach somebody who did that.”
Pentagon chief insists ‘Iran is devastated’
Hegseth reiterated that “Iran is devastated,” even though the Islamic Republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East that are used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Disruptions to shipping in the waterway, where one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war, have led to higher energy prices that hit voters’ pocketbooks.
He said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including telling Iran: “Hey, we’re done, and we’re going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it.”
Hegseth’s defense of the war comes after about 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.
With anger in Congress rising, Hegseth has been on a social media blitz, posting a video last week acknowledging the threat of impeachment. He said it would be “all about the politics of personal destruction” and insisted that “won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”
Since then, scores of political appointees within the Pentagon have posted images of Hegseth emblazoned with the words, “Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic.” The White House also posted a video to social media that featured praise from Trump.

A Republican lawmaker moved on Monday to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, setting up a potentially explosive vote in Congress just days after US President Donald Trump's party suffered a crushing midterm defeat.
Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorisation and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
The Republican-controlled House could vote as early as Wednesday, with some lawmakers from Trump's party signalling that they might join Democrats in supporting the charges.
Impeachment would be a humiliating blow for Hegseth and the Trump administration, but would not automatically remove him from office.
That would require a trial and conviction by a two-thirds majority in the Senate – a far higher hurdle, even after Democrats take control of the chamber in January.
The impeachment push has gathered momentum since last Tuesday's midterm elections, when Democrats swept both chambers of Congress amid widespread anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices.
Republicans retain control of Congress until the newly elected lawmakers take office on January 3, but their overwhelming defeat has fuelled recriminations and weakened party discipline.
Some Republican lawmakers who lost their seats could also skip votes, potentially making it easier for the impeachment measure to pass.
Massie, an outspoken critic of Trump who lost his own primary to a candidate backed by the president, is using a special congressional procedure to force the House to consider his resolution within two legislative days.
Republican leaders could still seek to block the measure through a procedural vote.
The articles accuse Hegseth of violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which limits the president's ability to engage US forces in hostilities without congressional approval.
They also allege misconduct involving civilian casualties and military operations in Yemen and Venezuela.
The Pentagon has rejected the accusations.
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker in January, threw his weight behind impeachment on Sunday.
"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC News.
"The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," he said.
"Pete Hegseth has got to go."
Several Republicans have expressed dissatisfaction with Hegseth's leadership without committing to impeaching him.
Arkansas congressman French Hill said on Sunday he wanted to hear the debate before deciding whether the accusations justified impeachment.
Under the US Constitution, the House can impeach a senior government official by a simple majority vote, effectively bringing formal charges of serious misconduct.
The Senate then decides whether to convict and remove the official from office, requiring support from two-thirds of senators present.
Even with their enlarged majority next year, Democrats would need substantial Republican backing to reach that threshold. Only two Cabinet secretaries – almost 150 years apart – have been impeached in US history, and neither was removed by the Senate.

Massie Forces Hegseth Impeachment Vote in House
sources.text:
Rep. Thomas Massie has forced a House vote on impeaching War Secretary Pete Hegseth, and some Republicans privately warn the privileged resolution could clear the chamber.
On Monday, the Kentucky Republican held the House floor for more than an hour and read out articles of impeachment against Hegseth. He used a privileged resolution, a procedure that requires the House to confront the measure within two legislative days, by Wednesday at the latest.
The drive lands after midterm elections in which Republicans took significant losses, with fallout from the war in Iran and high gas prices blamed as a key factor. Fox News reported that several House Republicans said Thursday they believe Hegseth could very well be impeached, even while a majority of the GOP conference is still expected to oppose the move.
House leaders can still try to table the resolution or send it to committee before a straight up-or-down vote. Either step would effectively kill it. It is not immediately clear which path GOP leaders will take.
Massie’s resolution carries eight articles. They cover the war in Iran, U.S. strikes against Yemen, strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean, and the extradition of now-former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Another article claims Hegseth retaliated against Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) over a video in which Kelly urged troops to resist “unlawful orders,” framing that dispute as an attack on free speech.
National Review detailed the same slate in sharper form: unauthorized Iran operations and War Powers Act timing fights; Houthi strikes without new approval from Congress; a strike in Minab that the articles say killed about 156 people, mostly children; boat strikes linked to at least 221 deaths, including alleged follow-on attacks on shipwrecked survivors; the Kelly matter; and the Venezuela operation that extracted Maduro.
Massie is not treating colleagues’ support for those missions as a defense. He lost his primary and will leave Congress in January, and he has criticized the Iran war from the start. Speaking as lawmakers returned to the Capitol, he drew a hard line between policy agreement and impeachment.
Rep. Thomas Massie told Just the News:
"I’ve seen some of my colleagues say [Secretary of War Pete] Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they’ll vote not to impeach. That’s not the question though. The question is whether he committed impeachable acts, and the answer is yes, eight times."
This is not Massie’s first attempt. He first introduced impeachment articles in September; they never received a vote. The Washington Examiner reported that the outgoing Republican reintroduced them Monday when Congress came back to Washington, kicking off what is expected to be heavy oversight of the Department of War after Democrats won control of both chambers in the midterms.
Last week, Massie told Fox News Digital he would trigger the vote when Congress returned after the elections if Hegseth did not resign first. Hegseth answered on Friday with a video on X. He called the impeachment effort a “shame” that “won’t work.”
The September filing leaned on the War Powers Resolution of 1973 and the claim that operations tied to Iran ran past the law’s limits without approval from Congress. The White House disputed the “war” label and the timeline math. The Justice Department and the Pentagon defended the secretary’s conduct.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said in remarks carried by the New York Post:
"Secretary Hegseth is doing a phenomenal job, and the secretary of war doesn’t just go off and do things. He follows the law."
Even some Republicans who disliked the Iran war are not signing up to impeach the secretary. Rep. Warren Davidson (R-Ohio), described as a critic of the war, told Fox News Digital he opposes impeaching Hegseth and cast the effort as misdirected accountability.
Rep. Warren Davidson said:
"I think it's an effort to scapegoat Pete Hegseth for Congress shirking their own duty and, frankly, the president taking action that, in my view, is unconstitutional, but it's also not unprecedented."
Davidson went further on the constitutional chain of command. He argued it would be unprecedented to punish the Pentagon chief for a presidential decision, and just as odd to expect a secretary to break ranks with a White House on force decisions that administrations have treated as standard practice back to the Korean War.
"What would be unprecedented is to hold the Secretary of Defense accountable for a decision the president makes," Davidson said. "Or frankly, it would have been unprecedented for the Secretary of Defense to kind of break ranks on something that is clearly not unprecedented in terms of what has become the standard operating procedure for administrations going back to the Korean War."
National Review’s Andrew C. McCarthy made the same structural point in legal terms. Impeaching a subordinate is allowed. Using that tool to avoid a fight over the president’s policy is another matter.
"While there is nothing illegal about impeaching a subordinate, doing so is a dodge if what’s at issue is the subordinate’s obeisant implementation of the president’s policy."
McCarthy added that Hegseth’s alleged sins are not freestanding personal misconduct. They are the execution of Trump’s directives.
Privileged status explains the sudden urgency. Leaders do not get an endless stall. They can still block a final judgment by tabling the resolution or referring it to committee, but they have to show their hand inside the two-day window.
The last Cabinet secretary impeached by the House was Biden-era Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas. Republicans charged him with dereliction of duty at the U.S.-Mexico border. That case died without a Senate trial once it reached a Democrat-controlled Senate.
Massie’s clock is shorter in a different way. He is on his way out of Congress. Democrats are preparing to run both chambers when the new Congress convenes. The lame-duck House still has to decide whether a Republican-led chamber will brand a sitting war secretary with impeachment articles over missions ordered by a Republican president.
Hegseth has already testified before the House Armed Services Committee and appeared with President Donald Trump at Camp David during a Cabinet meeting. The political question now is narrower: whether enough Republicans join Massie, or peel away under midterm pressure, to let the articles through before leaders can bury them.
If the House wants a real constitutional fight over war powers, it should have that fight with the office that sets the policy, not turn a Cabinet secretary into a convenient target for members who ducked the harder vote when it counted.

sources.text:
A Republican politician has moved to impeach US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, setting up a potentially explosive vote in Congress just days after President Donald Trump's party suffered a crushing midterm defeat.
Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment accusing Mr Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorisation and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
The Republican-controlled House could vote as early as Wednesday, with some politicians from Mr Trump's party signalling that they might join Democrats in supporting the charges.
Impeachment would be a humiliating blow for Mr Hegseth and the Trump administration, but would not automatically remove him from office.
That would require a trial and conviction by a two-thirds majority in the Senate -- a far higher hurdle, even after Democrats take control of the chamber in January.
The impeachment push has gathered momentum since Tuesday's midterm elections, when Democrats swept both chambers of Congress amid widespread anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices.
Republicans retain control of Congress until the newly elected politicians take office on 3 January, but their overwhelming defeat has fuelled recriminations and weakened party discipline.
Some Republicans who lost their seats could also skip votes, potentially making it easier for the impeachment measure to pass.
'Hard yes'
Mr Massie, an outspoken critic of Mr Trump who lost his own primary to a candidate backed by the president, is using a special congressional procedure to force the House to consider his resolution within two legislative days.
Republican leaders could still seek to block the measure through a procedural vote.
The articles accuse Mr Hegseth of violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which limits the president's ability to engage US forces in hostilities without congressional approval.
They also allege misconduct involving civilian casualties and military operations in Yemen and Venezuela.
The Pentagon has rejected the accusations.
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker in January, threw his weight behind impeachment yesterday.

Unlikely removal
Under the US Constitution, the House can impeach a senior government official by a simple majority vote, effectively bringing formal charges of serious misconduct.

Under legislative rules, the House of Representatives will have to take up a vote on the impeachment measure by Wednesday, according to the report.
Introducing the articles on the floor, Massie, an outgoing lawmaker and persistent critic of Trump, alleged that Hegseth had abused the power of his office through military actions taken during the conflict with Iran.
Massie claimed that the Defence Secretary had "knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation," CNN reported.
“Secretary of Defence Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law,” CNN quoted Massie as saying during the introduction of the resolution.
However, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio came out in strong support of Hegseth, asserting that he has "done a great job," CNN reported.
Speaking to reporters in Paris, where he is attending the G7 Foreign Ministers' meeting, Rubio pushed back against criticism directed at Hegseth from lawmakers and the media.
“I work with him, so I see perhaps a side of him that the media doesn’t see and members of Congress may not see,” CNN quoted Rubio as saying in defence of the Defence Secretary.
Earlier in the day, US President Donald Trump also pushed back against mounting congressional calls to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, questioning why an official instrumental to the military campaign against Iran should face removal from office.
Defending the administration’s armed intervention, the American leader asserted that United States strikes had successfully dismantled Iranian nuclear infrastructure while blocking Tehran from acquiring atomic capabilities.
“We saved Israel and the Middle East. There would be no Israel even if we had not saved them from Iran,” Trump said. Rejecting the impeachment initiative, he added, “And what are we going to do with one of the guys that was most responsible for the war, we want to impeach him.”
The presidential defence followed statements from House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries endorsing moves to impeach Hegseth, whom critics accused of abusing administrative authority, compromising national security and coordinating the conflict with Iran.
In an interview with ABC News, Jeffries confirmed his backing for an impeachment resolution drafted by Republican Representative Thomas Massie.
“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries stated, noting that House Democrats intended to review the measure upon returning to Capitol Hill on Tuesday.
“The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go,” Jeffries remarked.
Furthermore, the Democratic leader indicated that his party would pursue initiatives to conclude the ongoing conflict if Democrats secured control of the congressional majority in January, characterising the military engagement as an expensive venture that burdened ordinary citizens with higher living costs.
In response to the legislative pressure, Hegseth dismissed the impeachment campaign as politically motivated.
“It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that,” he said.
Representative Massie originally tabled the impeachment resolution against Hegseth in September, though congressional leadership subsequently shelved a scheduled floor vote, postponing consideration until the conclusion of the November midterm elections. (ANI)

sources.text:
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky began impeachment proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday, reading eight Articles of Impeachment on the House floor.
Massie, a longtime critic of the Trump administration, delivered a 34-page privileged resolution with the eight articles of impeachment. Privileged resolutions require the House to act on them, table them or vote to refer them to committee within two legislative days.
Massie originally introduced articles of impeachment in September, but a vote was postponed until this month after the chamber canceled its final day of work ahead of a lengthy recess.
Massie accused Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors. Three articles accuse him of abusing the powers of the Defense Department by waging war against Iran without congressional authorization.
“We’re not worried about that,” Hegseth, who gave a speech Monday at the Naval War College in Newport, R.I., told reporters traveling with him about the impeachment vote. “Actually … we’re going to do a press conference in the morning at the Pentagon on that very topic. So I’ll save my remarks there.”
The revived impeachment effort comes less than a week after Democrats swept to majorities in both houses of Congress in midterm elections. New members of Congress will be sworn in on Jan. 3.
In addition to the Iran war, Massie’s resolution charges Hegseth with ignoring laws to minimize civilian casualties.
The Pentagon has yet to release the findings of an investigation into the Feb. 28 airstrike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Iran. At least 168 people died in the attack, most of them children, according to Iranian state media.
Other articles of impeachment include: the strikes on alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean; suppressing the free speech of Sen. Trump stands by embattled Hegseth after Republican launches bid to impeach US defence chief
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump on Nov 9 threw his support behind embattled US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, declaring he had “won” wars in Venezuela and Iran.
Hours after a Republican lawmaker moved to impeach Hegseth on Nov 10, Trump defended Hegseth at a White House press briefing, saying: “Yeah, I’ll stand by him... He won two wars. He was in charge.”
Trump was speaking after Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie moved on Nov 9 to impeach Hegseth over the war in Iran, setting up a potentially explosive vote in Congress just days after Trump’s party suffered a crushing midterm defeat.
Kentucky congressman Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorisation and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
The Republican-controlled House could vote as early as Nov 11, with some lawmakers from Trump’s party signalling that they might join Democrats in backing those charges.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio came to Hegseth’s defence on Nov 9 while visiting Paris.
“I think it’s unfair. Look, I think Pete’s done a good job, I really do,” Rubio told reporters, praising his colleague as hardworking and “incredibly smart”.
Rubio credited Hegseth with helping build counter-cartel partnerships in the Americas, severely weakening Iran’s military and overseeing the operation to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro.
Impeachment would be a humiliating blow for Hegseth and the Trump administration, but would not automatically remove him from office.
That would require a trial and conviction by a two-thirds majority in the Senate – a far higher hurdle, even after Democrats take control of the chamber in January.
The impeachment push has gathered momentum since the Nov 3 midterm elections, when Democrats swept both chambers of Congress amid widespread anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices.
Republicans retain control of Congress until the newly elected lawmakers take office on Jan 3, but their overwhelming defeat has fuelled recriminations and weakened party discipline.
Some Republican lawmakers who lost their seats could also skip votes, potentially making it easier for the impeachment measure to pass.
‘Hard yes’
Massie, an outspoken critic of Trump who lost his own primary to a candidate backed by the President, is using a special congressional procedure to force the House to consider his resolution within two legislative days.
He said Hegseth had “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders” by starting a war without seeking authorisation from Congress, as he read the articles of impeachment on the House floor.
The articles accuse Hegseth of violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which limits the President’s ability to engage US forces in hostilities without congressional approval.
They also allege misconduct involving civilian casualties and military operations in Yemen and Venezuela.
The Pentagon has rejected the accusations.
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker in January, threw his weight behind impeachment on Nov 8.
“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries told ABC News. “The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.
“Pete Hegseth has got to go.”
Unlikely removal
Several Republicans have expressed dissatisfaction with Hegseth’s leadership without committing to impeaching him.
Arkansas congressman French Hill said on Nov 8 he wanted to hear the debate before deciding whether the accusations justified impeachment.
Under the US Constitution, the House can impeach a senior government official by a simple majority vote, effectively bringing formal charges of serious misconduct.
The Senate then decides whether to convict and remove the official from office, requiring support from two-thirds of senators present.
Even with their enlarged majority in 2027, Democrats would need substantial Republican backing to reach that threshold. Only two Cabinet secretaries – almost 150 years apart – have been impeached in US history, and neither was removed by the Senate.
Hegseth has dismissed Massie’s impeachment effort as a “sham”, calling the congressman “disgruntled” and accusing his opponents of pursuing political destruction.
The Pentagon announced a rare press briefing by Hegseth scheduled for Nov 10.
Trump has publicly stood by his embattled defence chief, declaring last week: “I have every intention to keep him.”
House Republican Don Bacon said he was uncomfortable with Massie’s reasoning, but argued that Hegseth should be impeached for withholding aid allocated to Ukraine and forcing out or blocking promotions for around 80 admirals and generals, an estimated 10% of the senior officer corps.
“And I’m not the only one feels this,” he told CNN, urging Hegseth to resign. “There’s a bunch of us have been talking about it.” AFP

WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing his fellow Republicans to remove one of the Trump administration’s most prominent figures following sweeping election losses blamed in part on fallout from the war in Iran.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican, read the impeachment resolution from the House floor just hours after it opened for the first day of sessions after the midterms. It largely focuses on the war in Iran but also includes references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
The congressman, who was defeated by a Trump-backed challenger in a primary earlier this year, said Hegseth’s actions amounted to “high crimes and misdemeanors.”
Hegseth, he said, “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders” and “remains a threat to the Constitution.”
President Donald Trump lashed out at Massie personally just hours after the congressman read the resolution, calling him a “loser” who “has a lot of hatred in his heart.”
A vote in the House could come by mid-week, but next steps are highly uncertain. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries supports the measure. If most Democrats follow him, Massie would only need support from a few Republicans to impeach Hegseth.
If the House votes to impeach, it would fall to to the Senate to either dismiss the charges or hold a trial. Republicans remain in the majority in both chambers, until the new Congress convenes in January with Democrats in control.
Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Democratic leader, endorsed the impeachment push. “Hegseth must stand trial before the Senate,” he said.
Republican leaders, who are eager to use their final weeks in power executing their own agenda, expressed frustration at the move. House Speaker Mike Johnson, who has tried to prevent the vote, said impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that.”
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he wasn’t sure why the vote was being held now.
“We’ll see what their ultimate decision is over there,” he said of the House. “We’ll have to deal with it accordingly here.”
Hegseth issues his own defense and prepares for a fight
Hegseth is stepping up his public statements ahead of the vote, telling reporters that he’s eager to defend the military actions that he and Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela’s previous leaders.
After giving a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, he brushed aside the impeachment push.
“There’s a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success,” he told reporters. He added that “if we want to litigate” the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, “I’m happy to do it all day long.”
Asked about Vice President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the massive GOP losses in the election, Hegseth noted that Trump said he would do it again, and “I agree.”
Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference on Tuesday — his first in over 180 days — on the impeachment threat.
Hegseth argued that the war was necessary because “someone had to confront the Iranian regime’s pursuit of a nuclear weapon” and said “the choice was don’t act and wish it away or take a bold move.”
Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Monday, commending him for having “won the war” in Venezuela and “winning the war” in Iran, which continues to drag on.
Pentagon chief insists ‘Iran is devastated’
Hegseth reiterated that “Iran is devastated,” even though the Islamic Republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East that are used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Disruptions to shipping in the waterway, where one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war, have led to higher energy prices that hit voters’ pocketbooks.
Hegseth’s defense of the war comes after about 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended his fellow Cabinet secretary, saying that he believes Hegesth has been doing “a great job” and that its unfair that a Republican is pushing the impeachment effort.
“I work with him. And so I see perhaps a side of him that the media doesn’t see and members of Congress may not see,” Rubio told reporters at the Group of Seven industrialized democracies gathering in Paris. “But I think Pete works really hard. He’s incredibly smart.”
Associated Press writers Kevin Freking, Lisa Mascaro, Joey Cappelletti and Farnoush Amiri contributed to this report.

"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Massie said. "Secretary Hegseth's constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran. He is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders, and to intimidate critics of the Trump administration by retaliating against them for exercising free speech. If we are to remain true to our oath to 'support and defend the Constitution of the United States,' the House of Representatives must act."
According to a release the impeachment charges are as follows:
- Article I - Waging War in Contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 Section 2(c): Charges Secretary Hegseth with waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat. It establishes that the war was unlawful from its inception.
- Article II - Waging War in Contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 Section 5(c): Charges Secretary Hegseth with continuing the Iran war after both Houses of Congress directed the removal of U.S. forces through H. Con. Res. 86. It focuses on his refusal to obey Congress’s express direction to terminate unauthorized hostilities.
- Article III - Waging War in Contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 Section 5(b): Charges Secretary Hegseth with continuing hostilities in Iran after expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period. It establishes that he treated mandatory statutory deadlines as discretionary.
- Article IV - Ignoring Laws that Minimize Civilian Casualties: Charges Secretary Hegseth with ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties.

It also addresses denial of quarter, secondary strikes on survivors, failure to rescue shipwrecked persons, and the creation of artificial legal authorities for the campaign.
- Article VI - Suppressing Free Speech: Charges Secretary Hegseth with using DOD authority to retaliate against and intimidate Senator Mark Kelly for constitutionally protected speech questioning unlawful military orders.
- Article VII - Kidnapping of a Sovereign Foreign Leader: Charges Secretary Hegseth with directing Operation ABSOLUTE RESOLVE to seize Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores in Venezuela without constitutional or legal authority.
- Article VIII - Unlawful War in Yemen: Charges Secretary Hegseth with initiating Operation ROUGH RIDER without congressional authorization or an imminent threat to the United States, while also violating war powers reporting requirements.
Hegseth argued that starting the war with Iran was a “bold move” by Trump “and as the president points out so clearly -- you can’t let crazy Islamists have a nuclear bomb.”
“The choice was don’t act and wish it away or take a bold move, which the president did with Midnight Hammer, which we’ve done with Epic Fury,” Hegseth said, referring to the code names for the strike on Iranian nuclear facilities and the larger war.
